title: Choose generic type parameters and constraints without replacing type safety with object casts

questions.prompt:
A conversion helper must accept a value and a conversion function, then return the function's result. One use converts a `string` into an `int`; another converts a `DateTime` into a `string`.

Consider this contract:
```csharp
TOutput Convert<TInput, TOutput>(
    TInput value,
    Func<TInput, TOutput> converter);
```
Explain why it uses two type parameters, how they let the compiler check the conversion, and what protection would be lost if the value, function input and result all used `object`.

rubric.point: Explains that input and output can have different types; using one shared T would require them to be the same type.
Explains that the function accepts TInput and returns TOutput, linking the supplied value and returned result through compiler-checked types.
Explains that an object-based contract loses these specific type relationships, requiring casts that can fail at runtime.

questions.model:
`TInput` and `TOutput` represent separate roles because a conversion can change the type, such as from `string` to `int`. One shared `T` would require the input and result to have the same type.

`Func<TInput, TOutput>` connects the converter's input to the value's type and its output to the helper's return type. The compiler checks those relationships, and the caller receives a typed result without a cast.

With `object` throughout, the signature does not express which input type the converter needs or which result type it produces. A converter might cast its input to `string` even though the helper accepts an integer. Such casts can compile and then fail at runtime.

rubric.point: States that new() requires a non-abstract type with a public parameterless constructor, allowing new T().
Explains that class guarantees only a reference type, not an accessible parameterless constructor, so it does not permit new T().
Explains that adding class excludes structs even though they can satisfy new() and the implementation does not require reference-type behavior.

questions.model:
`new()` requires a non-abstract type with a public parameterless constructor. That gives the compiler the guarantee needed for `new T()`.

`class` only requires a reference type. A class might have only constructors with arguments, so `class` alone does not make `new T()` legal.

Adding `class` to `new()` would exclude structs. Structs can satisfy `new()`, and this factory only needs to construct and return a value; it has no requirement for reference-type behavior.
